bibl.title: Plastic Pollution in the World's Oceans: More than 5 Trillion Plastic Pieces Weighing over 250,000 Tons Afloat at Sea

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: the count and weight of plastic particles floating at the surface of the world's oceans, in four size classes
span.quote: Based on our model results, we estimate that at least 5.25 trillion plastic particles weighing 268,940 tons are currently floating at sea (Table 1). There was a good correspondence between the model prediction and measured data for particle count and weight (Figs. S1 and S2, Table S4).

span.label: how much plastic is afloat in the world's oceans, and whether the size distribution matches what fragmentation of larger items predicts
span.quote: When comparing between four size classes, two microplastic <4.75 mm and meso- and macroplastic >4.75 mm, a tremendous loss of microplastics is observed from the sea surface compared to expected rates of fragmentation, suggesting there are mechanisms at play that remove <4.75 mm plastic particles from the ocean surface.

span.label: a global estimate across all four size classes - at least 5.25 trillion particles weighing 268,940 tons - and the finding that microplastics are an order of magnitude scarcer than fragmentation predicts
span.quote: Based on our model results, we estimate that at least 5.25 trillion plastic particles weighing 268,940 tons are currently floating at sea (Table 1). There was a good correspondence between the model prediction and measured data for particle count and weight (Figs. S1 and S2, Table S4).

span.label: existence
span.quote: Based on our model results, we estimate that at least 5.25 trillion plastic particles weighing 268,940 tons are currently floating at sea (Table 1). There was a good correspondence between the model prediction and measured data for particle count and weight (Figs. S1 and S2, Table S4).

span.label: differential loss of small microplastics from the sea surface
span.quote: When comparing between four size classes, two microplastic <4.75 mm and meso- and macroplastic >4.75 mm, a tremendous loss of microplastics is observed from the sea surface compared to expected rates of fragmentation, suggesting there are mechanisms at play that remove <4.75 mm plastic particles from the ocean surface.

span.label: surface net tows and visual transects at 1571 locations, fitted to an oceanographic particle-tracking model and corrected for wind-driven vertical mixing
span.term: surface net tows and visual transects at 1571 locations, fitted to an oceanographic particle-tracking model and corrected for wind-driven vertical mixing
span.quote: The oceanographic model assumes that amounts of plastic entering the ocean depend on three principal variables: watershed outfalls, population density and maritime activity.

span.label: UV degradation, biodegradation, ingestion by organisms, loss of buoyancy from fouling, entrainment in settling detritus and beaching all take small particles out of the sampled layer
span.quote: The observations that there is much less microplastic at the sea surface than might be expected suggests that removal processes are at play. These include UV degradation, biodegradation, ingestion by organisms, decreased buoyancy due to fouling organisms, entrainment in settling detritus, and beaching.

span.label: brittle microplastics may break down faster than they are replaced, into particles smaller than the 0.33 mm mesh, so they leave the measurement rather than the ocean
span.quote: Fragmentation rates of already brittle microplastics may be very high, rapidly breaking small microplastics further down into ever smaller particles, making them unavailable for our nets (0.33 mm mesh opening).

span.label: as a particle shrinks its surface-area-to-volume ratio rises sharply and oxidation increases, so microbial degradation accelerates at exactly the sizes that are missing
span.quote: This process becomes more important as plastic particles become smaller since at decreasing particle size the surface area∶volume relationship is increased dramatically and oxidation levels are higher, enhancing their biodegradation potential.

span.label: the fragmentation accounting assumes the system is near equilibrium, and inputs and outputs of ocean plastic are unknown
span.quote: This stepwise approach is simplistic, because it assumes that the system is close to equilibrium. We recognize that rates of new plastic entering the ocean are unknown, as well as outputs of plastic due to beaching, sinking and mechanisms of degradation, and use these fragmentation estimates as first crude intent to reveal the dynamics of floating plastics in the oceans.

span.label: the estimates are conservative and should be read as minima; macroplastic rests on a limited inventory of observations
span.quote: However, we stress that our estimates are highly conservative, and may be considered minimum estimates. Our estimates of macroplastic are based on a limited inventory of ocean observations, and would be vastly improved with standardization of methods and more observations.

span.label: plastic on shorelines, on the seabed, in the water column and inside organisms is not counted at all
span.quote: They also do not account for the potentially massive amount of plastic present on shorelines, on the seabed, suspended in the water column, and within organisms.

span.label: where the missing plastic goes is left open - the paper closes on the question rather than an answer
span.quote: By generating extensive new data, especially from the Southern Hemisphere, and modeling the plastic load in the world's oceans in separate size classes, we show that there is tremendous loss of microplastics from the sea surface. The question “Where is all the Plastic?” remains unanswered, highlighting the need to investigate the many processes that play a role in the dynamics of macro-, meso- and microplastics in the world's oceans.

span.label: the surface-area-to-volume argument, taken from microbial ecology to explain why the smallest particles vanish fastest
span.quote: This process becomes more important as plastic particles become smaller since at decreasing particle size the surface area∶volume relationship is increased dramatically and oxidation levels are higher, enhancing their biodegradation potential.

span.label: conservative weights assigned to the two catch-all visual-survey categories
span.note: eliminates: an unweighted catch-all category dominating a global mass estimate through the items nobody could identify · outcome: held
span.quote: The two categories labeled ‘other fishing gear’ and ‘miscellaneous plastics’ were assigned a very conservative weight of 10 g per item.

span.label: fragmentation parameters chosen so the predicted particle counts are under-stated rather than over-stated
span.note: eliminates: a fragmentation model tuned until it produced the particle count the survey found - the bias is set to under-state on purpose, so agreement cannot be manufactured · outcome: held
span.quote: Thus, our fragmentation estimates are highly conservative because for the macroplastics that generate plastic fragments we consider lower initial mass than commonly found at sea, while for the microplastics in our fragmentation exercise we consider larger particles than typically found at sea.

span.label: correction for wind-driven vertical mixing carrying particles below the sampled layer
span.note: eliminates: surface sampling being read as total abundance when wind drives particles below the sampled layer · outcome: held
span.quote: Wind-driven mixing of the surface layer will drive particles downward, which causes underestimations of plastic in the ocean if relying on surface sampling only.

span.label: the global microplastic estimate checked against two independent published estimates
span.note: eliminates: a global estimate resting on one team's method with no independent magnitude to check it against · outcome: held
span.quote: Other estimates of global and regional weight of microplastic pollution are within the same order of magnitude as our estimates. A study using an 11-year data set in the North Pacific estimates a weight of 21,290 metric tons of floating microplastic, and ours for the same region is 12,100 metric tons. A recent study on the global distribution of microplastic suggests that the total floating microplastic load ranges between 7,000 and 35,000 metric tons, and ours is 35,500 metric tons.

span.label: an accounting of plastic on shorelines, on the seabed, in the water column and within organisms
span.note: eliminates: plastic that is not floating at the surface - shorelines, seabed, water column and organisms are outside the estimate, so the total is a count of one compartment presented against a question about the ocean · outcome: absent-declared-unreported
span.quote: They also do not account for the potentially massive amount of plastic present on shorelines, on the seabed, suspended in the water column, and within organisms.

span.label: microplastic
span.quote: We have used 4.75 mm as our upper boundary for microplastic because this is a size for standard sieves used for sample analysis in most of the expeditions contributing data to this manuscript.

span.label: mesoplastic
span.quote: Mesoplastic has a lower limit of 4.75 mm, and no defined upper limit. In this current study we set the upper boundary of mesoplastic at 200 mm, which represents a typical plastic water bottle, chosen because of its ubiquity in the ocean. Macroplastic has no established lower boundary, though we set it at 200 mm, while the upper boundary is unlimited.

span.label: Macroplastic
span.quote: Mesoplastic has a lower limit of 4.75 mm, and no defined upper limit. In this current study we set the upper boundary of mesoplastic at 200 mm, which represents a typical plastic water bottle, chosen because of its ubiquity in the ocean. Macroplastic has no established lower boundary, though we set it at 200 mm, while the upper boundary is unlimited.

span.label: neuston net
span.quote: The prefixes micro, meso and macro in relation to plastic pollution are poorly defined. Generally accepted microplastic boundaries are based on typical neuston net mesh size (0.33 mm) and an upper boundary of approximately 5.0 mm.

span.label: fragmentation
span.quote: The expected numbers of microplastics (large and small) were an order of magnitude larger than the data-calibrated model counts of microplastics in the world's oceans (Fig. S3). The expected numbers were derived from conservative estimates of fragmentation from macroplastic to smaller size classes.

span.label: vertical distribution
span.quote: ### Adjusting estimated weight and count due to vertical distribution Wind-driven mixing of the surface layer will drive particles downward, which causes underestimations of plastic in the ocean if relying on surface sampling only.

span.label: ultimate sink
span.quote: In fact, the larger weight of macroplastic relative to meso- and microplastic, and the global estimate of floating plastic weight relative to the weight of plastic produced annually, indicates that the sea surface is likely not the ultimate sink for plastic pollution.

span.label: sea surface
span.quote: The observations that there is much less microplastic at the sea surface than might be expected suggests that removal processes are at play. These include UV degradation, biodegradation, ingestion by organisms, decreased buoyancy due to fouling organisms, entrainment in settling detritus, and beaching.

span.label: the prefixes micro, meso and macro are POORLY DEFINED in this field - stated by the authors
span.quote: The prefixes micro, meso and macro in relation to plastic pollution are poorly defined. Generally accepted microplastic boundaries are based on typical neuston net mesh size (0.33 mm) and an upper boundary of approximately 5.0 mm.

span.label: microplastic upper bound = 4.75 mm BECAUSE IT IS A STANDARD SIEVE SIZE, not a property of plastic
span.quote: We have used 4.75 mm as our upper boundary for microplastic because this is a size for standard sieves used for sample analysis in most of the expeditions contributing data to this manuscript.

span.label: mesoplastic upper bound = 200 mm BECAUSE THAT IS A TYPICAL PLASTIC WATER BOTTLE
span.quote: Mesoplastic has a lower limit of 4.75 mm, and no defined upper limit. In this current study we set the upper boundary of mesoplastic at 200 mm, which represents a typical plastic water bottle, chosen because of its ubiquity in the ocean. Macroplastic has no established lower boundary, though we set it at 200 mm, while the upper boundary is unlimited.

span.label: macroplastic lower bound = 200 mm, set by this paper because the field has no established one
span.quote: Mesoplastic has a lower limit of 4.75 mm, and no defined upper limit. In this current study we set the upper boundary of mesoplastic at 200 mm, which represents a typical plastic water bottle, chosen because of its ubiquity in the ocean. Macroplastic has no established lower boundary, though we set it at 200 mm, while the upper boundary is unlimited.

span.label: the boundaries are LOGISTIC rather than conceptual - net and sieve sizes - and are declared as such
span.quote: There is a clear need for consistent measures in the field, and herein we followed a practical approach using commonly employed boundaries and logistic considerations (net and sieve sizes) in order to integrate an extensive dataset that covers the entire global ocean, including areas that have never been sampled before.

span.label: the field's generally accepted lower bound, 0.33 mm, is a neuston net's mesh opening
span.quote: The prefixes micro, meso and macro in relation to plastic pollution are poorly defined. Generally accepted microplastic boundaries are based on typical neuston net mesh size (0.33 mm) and an upper boundary of approximately 5.0 mm.

span.quote: Plastic pollution is ubiquitous throughout the marine environment, yet estimates of the global abundance and weight of floating plastics have lacked data, particularly from the Southern Hemisphere and remote regions.

span.label: confirms → an independent study reporting a large discrepancy between expected and observed microplastic
span.note: the agreement is used as support for the hypothesis, not merely as a consistency check
span.quote: The similarities between our results and those of this study gives us further confidence in our estimates and support our hypothesis that the ultimate fate of buoyant microplastics is not at the ocean surface.

span.note: direction on the measure: reduces · strength of the relation: 0.85
span.quote: Before using the vertical distribution equation, we transformed these data into wind stress values, by applying the Smith coefficient for sea surface wind stress (N/m2) as a function of wind speed (m/s).

span.label: microplastics are an order of magnitude scarcer than conservative fragmentation estimates predict
span.quote: The expected numbers of microplastics (large and small) were an order of magnitude larger than the data-calibrated model counts of microplastics in the world's oceans (Fig. S3). The expected numbers were derived from conservative estimates of fragmentation from macroplastic to smaller size classes.

span.label: the smallest microplastics are LESS abundant than larger ones, the opposite of what fragmentation implies, in every region but the South Pacific
span.quote: Most small microplastics were fragments resulting from the breakdown of larger plastic items; therefore we expected the smallest microplastics to be more abundant than larger microplastics. We observed the opposite in all regions globally except in the S. Pacific where large and small microplastic counts were nearly equal.

span.quote: In fact, the larger weight of macroplastic relative to meso- and microplastic, and the global estimate of floating plastic weight relative to the weight of plastic produced annually, indicates that the sea surface is likely not the ultimate sink for plastic pollution.

Our data suggest that a minimum of 233,400 tons of larger plastic items are afloat in the world's oceans compared to 35,540 tons of microplastics.

Our estimate of the global weight of plastic pollution on the sea surface, from all size classes combined, is only 0.1% of the world annual production.
